title: Optimal approximation ratio for unrelated-machine makespan
formal: Determine \(\rho _{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\){\(r\ge 1: a\) uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible solution of objective value at most \(r\cdot\)OPT on every unrelated-machine scheduling instance}, in the input and output model below.
definitions: An instance consists of \(m\ge 1\) machines, \(n\ge 0\) independent jobs, and an explicitly given \(m\times n\) matrix of processing times \(p_{ij}\) in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function \(\sigma :\{1,\ldots ,n\}\to \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(p_{\sigma (j),j}<\infty\). Its makespan is \(Cmax(\sigma )=\max _{i} \sum_{j:\sigma (j)=i} p_{ij}\), and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output \(\sigma\), not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. For each fixed achieved ratio r, the algorithm and its time polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object. For each fixed ratio r in the defining set, one finite deterministic algorithm and one time polynomial must work on every instance; both may depend on r. The infimum is over these globally uniform guarantees and need not be attained. There is no per-input-size choice of algorithm, advice or free optimization oracle.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \rho _{\mathrm{unrel}}|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture. Any hardness assumption must be stated explicitly; a conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion.
why: A defining unresolved approximation barrier in scheduling. Beating two by any fixed constant would also imply a constant approximation for general Santa Claus allocation, while known relaxation gaps rule out a large family of straightforward proofs.

importance.reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.

progress.text: Lenstra–Shmoys–Tardos establish a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation and hardness below \(3/2\) unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
Shchepin–Vakhania achieve \(2- 1/m\). The saving vanishes as the number of machines grows.
Verschae–Wiese show that the configuration LP has integrality gap two even for unrelated graph balancing.
Bamas and coauthors reduce constant-factor Santa Claus approximation to a constant improvement over two for unrelated makespan, and give stronger special-case algorithms.
Baba–Bampis–Mitropoulos obtain improved prediction-sensitive guarantees with worst-case factor two; the unconditional classical barrier remains.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The full worst-case constant-improvement question remains open in the checked primary literature. The known \(2- 1/m\) ratio and prediction-assisted results have different quantifiers from the fixed-\(\varepsilon\) target. The \(3/2\) hardness is conditional on \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The target is the infimum polynomial-time approximation ratio. The factor-two algorithmic question discussed in the saved history selects one threshold in this larger numerical target.

Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with \(p_{ij}>T\) are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below \(3/2\). This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to \(2- 1/m\). That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. Beating the universal infimum two requires one fixed improvement independent of machine count; a \(2- 1/m\) guarantee alone does not give that.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time \(p_{j}\) on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time \((1.75+\delta )\)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives \(2- 1/n\)ᵟ for fixed \(\delta >0\), whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A \((2- 1/\alpha )\)-approximation for makespan, for constant \(\alpha \ge 2\), would yield an \((\alpha +\delta )\)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed \(\delta >0\). Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.
